Serpent (Doctrine)
SUR-pent
n.
Latin serpens, “creeping thing”; Hebrew nāchāsh (serpent, possibly related to nāchash, to divine, suggesting the serpent’s association with hidden knowledge); Greek ophis (serpent). One of the most extensive metaphors in Scripture, governing Satan’s first appearance in Genesis 3, the brazen serpent of Numbers 21, and Christ’s teaching on the wise-as-serpents disciple.

📖 Biblical Definition

The serpent is one of the most extensive and theologically loaded metaphors in Scripture, running from Genesis 3 through Revelation 20 as the principal symbol of Satan and his work, with various other biblical uses (the brazen serpent, the disciple’s wisdom-as-serpents) that fold into the larger doctrinal pattern. Genesis 3 opens the doctrine: now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made. And he said unto the woman, Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden? The serpent in Eden is identified as Satan’s instrument (Rev 12:9; 20:2 explicitly: the great dragon was cast out, that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan); the tempter who introduces sin into the human race through deception about God’s word. Genesis 3:15 establishes the protoevangelium: and I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel. The serpent’s defeat at the cross (the head-crushing of the seed of the woman, fulfilled supremely in Christ) is announced at the very moment of the original temptation. Numbers 21:6-9 records the brazen serpent: when fiery serpents bit Israel in the wilderness, the LORD instructed Moses to make a serpent of brass and set it on a pole; everyone who looked upon the brazen serpent lived. Christ Himself applies this directly to Himself in John 3:14-15: and as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up: That whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life. The brazen serpent on the pole prefigured Christ on the cross: the look-and-live principle of OT typology fulfilled in the look-to-Christ-and-be-saved principle of the gospel. (The brazen serpent was eventually destroyed by Hezekiah, who broke it in pieces and called it Nehushtan, a brass-thing, because Israel had begun to burn incense to it as an idol—2 Kgs 18:4—a warning that even divinely-appointed sacred objects can become idolatrous when divorced from their proper context.) Christ’s teaching in Matthew 10:16: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves—the serpent’s wisdom (its alertness, its careful navigation of hostile territory, its strategic shrewdness) is to be combined with the dove’s harmlessness in the disciple’s witness. Revelation closes the canonical-serpent-doctrine: the great dragon, that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world, is bound for a thousand years and finally cast into the lake of fire (Rev 20:2, 10). The serpent-doctrine therefore traces a complete arc: introduced as the tempter in Eden, defeated typologically through the brazen serpent and substantively at the cross, providing a model of strategic wisdom for the disciple, and finally cast into the eternal punishment that completes the protoevangelium’s head-crushing promise.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SERPENT as an animal of the order Ophidia, without feet; in scripture, the great metaphor of Satan from Genesis 3 onward (cf. Rev 12:9; 20:2), the brazen serpent of Numbers 21 typologically anticipating Christ on the cross (John 3:14), and the wise-as-serpents model for the disciple’s witness (Matt 10:16).

SERPENT, n. — 1. An animal of the order Ophidia, without feet, moving by undulations along the ground. 2. In scripture, applied to Satan (Gen 3; Rev 12:9), to the brazen serpent of Num 21 (typologically anticipating Christ in John 3:14), and to the strategic wisdom of the disciple (Matt 10:16).

BRAZEN SERPENT — The serpent of brass set on a pole by Moses in Num 21, by looking on which the bitten Israelites were healed; typologically fulfilled in Christ lifted up on the cross (John 3:14-15).

📖 Key Scripture

Genesis 3:1 — "Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made. And he said unto the woman, Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?"

Genesis 3:15 — "And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel."

John 3:14-15 — "And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up: That whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life."

Revelation 20:2 — "And he laid hold on the dragon, that old serpent, which is the Devil, and Satan, and bound him a thousand years."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The serpent-doctrine is corrupted, on one side, by the demythologizing tradition that has treated the Genesis 3 serpent as merely literary symbol rather than as Satan’s actual instrument (against the NT’s explicit identifications)—and on the other by the over-extension of the wise-as-serpents instruction into pragmatic-political shrewdness without the dove’s pairing-harmlessness Christ explicitly couples it with.

expand to see more

The demythologizing tradition has often treated the Genesis 3 serpent as merely literary symbol—a personification of inner temptation, a folk-tale device, a mythopoetic figure—rather than as Satan’s actual instrument of temptation as the New Testament repeatedly identifies him. Rev 12:9 is explicit: and the great dragon was cast out, that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world: he was cast out into the earth, and his angels were cast out with him. Rev 20:2 is similarly explicit. 2 Cor 11:3 connects Eve’s deception to the serpent and warns of the same kind of deception of the church. The New Testament refuses the demythologization; the serpent is Satan’s instrument, Satan is a personal being, the temptation in Eden was a historical event, and the protoevangelium of Gen 3:15 is the substantive promise the cross has fulfilled. The recovery is the recovery of biblical realism about Satan, his agency, his temptations, and his defeat by Christ.

The opposite corruption is the over-extension of Christ’s wise-as-serpents instruction into pragmatic-political shrewdness without the dove’s pairing-harmlessness Christ explicitly couples it with. The instruction reads: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves. Both parts are required. The serpent’s wisdom alone, without the dove’s harmlessness, produces the shrewd-but-unprincipled operator—the Christian who has learned strategic effectiveness and lost moral purity, the political-religious figure whose tactics are sharp and whose conscience has become accommodating. Christ’s pairing prevents this. The disciple is to be alert, strategically aware, careful in navigating hostile territory (the serpent’s wisdom)—and also harmless, pure, blameless in his own actions and dealings (the dove’s harmlessness). To pursue serpent-wisdom apart from dove-harmlessness is to fall into the shrewd-but-corrupt pattern; to pursue dove-harmlessness apart from serpent-wisdom is to fall into the well-meaning-but-naive pattern. Recover both. The biblical serpent-doctrine refuses both extremes: Satan’s serpent in Eden is the historical adversary the Christ has overcome, and the disciple’s serpent-wisdom is to be balanced by dove-harmlessness in the practical pattern Christ Himself prescribed.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew nāchāsh (serpent); Greek ophis (serpent); the extensive biblical metaphor running from Genesis 3 (Satan’s instrument) through Numbers 21 (the brazen serpent typologically anticipating Christ on the cross—John 3:14) and Matthew 10:16 (the wise-as-serpents disciple) to Revelation 20:2 (the old serpent’s final defeat).

expand to see more

Hebrew nāchāsh (H5175) — serpent (over 30 OT uses; Gen 3; Num 21; 2 Kgs 18:4).

Greek ophis (G3789) — serpent (14 NT uses; Matt 10:16; John 3:14; 2 Cor 11:3; Rev 12:9; 20:2).

Hebrew n’chush-tan (H5180) — Nehushtan (the brass-thing, the brazen serpent later worshipped as an idol; 2 Kgs 18:4).

Greek drakōn (G1404) — dragon (the Revelation title for Satan, identified explicitly with the old serpent in Rev 12:9; 20:2).

Usage

"The seed of the woman shall bruise the serpent’s head—Gen 3:15’s protoevangelium announces the serpent’s coming defeat at the very moment of the original temptation."

"As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up—Christ’s explicit application of the brazen-serpent typology to His crucifixion (John 3:14-15)."

"Demythologization denies the personal-Satan reality; wise-as-serpents-without-dove pursues shrewdness without harmlessness; biblical doctrine holds personal-Satan-overcome-by-Christ alongside the wise-and-harmless disciple-pairing."
